summary: Describes a security model for using tunnel-mode IPsec on devices that perform network address translation. It explains how IPsec can be arranged so that a NAT device takes part in securing traffic between domains. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Imagine a mail room that swaps return addresses and also seals letters in locked boxes. This explains how to do both without breaking anything.

questions: how to use ipsec tunnel mode with nat
how can nat and ipsec work together
subtitle: How network address translation and IPsec can work together to protect traffic from private networks.

tldr.problem: Private networks protected by NAT devices need security for traffic sent to external networks, but NAT and IPsec encryption have conflicting requirements.
tldr.mechanism: IPsec Policy Controlled NAT (IPC-NAT) applies address translation to packets inside IPsec tunnels, allowing NAT devices to act as IPsec gateways. This works by applying security policies before address translation.
tldr.outcome: A NAT device can now provide tunnel-mode IPsec encryption to all its private domain hosts, enabling secure connections to external networks and secure remote access for mobile users.

today: RFC 2709 is informational and has not been obsoleted. It describes a security architecture that has been widely adopted in enterprise VPN and remote access scenarios.

sections.title: Introduction: NAT and Security
sections.content:
Network Address Translation (NAT) lets private networks communicate with the public Internet by replacing internal IP addresses with external ones as traffic passes through. However, private hosts need encryption when talking to external networks, and encryption conflicts with address translation since NAT must read and modify IP headers.

This RFC solves the problem with a model where the NAT device itself becomes an IPsec gateway, protecting all traffic leaving the private network without requiring end-to-end encryption from individual hosts.
sections.eli5: NAT is like a mail room that rewrites return addresses. IPsec is like sealed envelopes. Normally, you cannot seal an envelope (encrypt) and then rewrite the return address, because you would have to open it first. This explains how to do both.

sections.title: Two Types of NAT Translation
sections.content:
Normal-NAT is standard address translation: the NAT device changes the IP address of outgoing packets and forwards them in the clear.

IPC-NAT (IPsec Policy Controlled NAT) extends this: the NAT device first applies IPsec encryption to create a tunnel, then applies address translation to the packets inside the tunnel. This is only done for packets matched by security policies. Other packets continue through Normal-NAT. Both types coexist on the same NAT device.
sections.eli5: Normal-NAT rewrites addresses on all packets. IPC-NAT first locks packets in IPsec boxes, then rewrites the addresses on those boxes. Regular packets that do not need locking skip the IPsec step.

sections.title: How IPC-NAT Works
sections.content:
When a packet arrives at an IPC-NAT device, the device checks if it matches an outbound security policy. If not, it is either forwarded in the clear or dropped. If it matches, the device performs address translation specific to that policy, then applies IPsec encryption. The encrypted packet is then sent to the external peer.

For incoming packets from the external realm, the device first removes the IPsec encryption (detunnels), then applies inbound address translation specific to the policy, and finally checks if the packet matches inbound security policies before forwarding.
sections.eli5: For outgoing mail: check if it needs a lock, lock it if yes, rewrite the return address, send it. For incoming mail: unlock it, rewrite the destination address, check if it is allowed, deliver it.

sections.title: Automated Key Exchange with IKE
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol automates the negotiation of IPsec session keys and security policies between two nodes. IKE operates in two phases: the first authenticates peers and sets up a secure channel; the second negotiates the security policies and parameters.

On an IPC-NAT device, the challenge is translating security policies from private realm addressing to external addressing before communicating them to peers. An IKE-ALG (an application-level gateway) performs this translation using the NAT mappings, so the external peer receives policies expressed in external addressing.
sections.eli5: Two parties need to agree on which packets to lock and which keys to use. IKE-ALG translates the private side's rules (with private addresses) into external side's rules (with external addresses) before asking the other party to agree.

sections.title: Real-World Uses
sections.content:
Secure Extranet Connectivity: A NAT device at the border of a private network can establish a secure IPsec tunnel to an external gateway, protecting all traffic crossing the Internet between the two domains.

Secure Remote Access: A mobile employee using a temporary address can establish an IPsec tunnel to the corporate NAT device. The device translates the mobile's temporary address into a corporate address, making it appear to internal servers as if the traffic came from inside the enterprise. This works because many enterprise applications rely on source IP addresses for access control.
sections.eli5: Extranet: two offices in different cities create a locked tunnel between their mail rooms. Remote Access: a traveling employee locks messages to the home mail room, which then rewrites them to look like they came from inside the office.
